Explainer-How Ukraine’s strikes on Russian energy sites deepened the rift with Trump

25 October, 2026 04:00 pm IST

By Simon Lewis and Steve Holland WASHINGTON, Oct 25 (Reuters) – Relations between US President Donald Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy took a sharp downward turn in recent weeks, with each leader openly criticizing the other. The two have long had a testy relationship, but Trump’s frustration over Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure triggered a crisis that Kyiv’s supporters fear could threaten vital US support going forward.

Here’s how the relationship soured:

WHAT IS THE HISTORY OF TRUMP-ZELENSKIY TENSIONS?

Show Full Article

Trump has been skeptical of US involvement in Ukraine ever since his first term when, shortly after taking office in early 2017, he was asked to provide lethal aid to Ukraine and approved the sale of Javelin missiles to Kyiv.

“Everyone around him wanted him to do it, and they pushed him hard and he eventually signed off on selling them Javelins, very reluctantly,” said a former senior Trump administration official, who spoke on condition of anonymity. “He didn’t consider it a core US interest. It was a European issue.”

Trump’s first major encounter with Zelenskiy came in a July 2019 phone call in which the Republican president asked the Ukrainian leader to investigate his Democratic rival Joe Biden and his son Hunter, in exchange for military support Congress had authorized.

That episode led to Trump’s first impeachment. Biden beat Trump in the 2020 presidential election.

Trump also has fostered a relationship with Russian President Vladimir Putin that runs against the norms of US foreign policy but echoes his warm ties with authoritarian leaders Xi Jinping of China and North Korea’s leader Kim Jong Un.

“Trump has always wanted better relations with Russia,” the former official said.

WHAT DEEPENED THE RIFT BETWEEN THE TWO LEADERS?

Trump’s current frustration centers on Kyiv’s attacks on Russian diesel infrastructure.

Diesel prices have hit record highs since the US and Israel launched a war against Iran in February, and global energy costs spiked. US lawmakers in Trump’s Republican party face voter anger over inflation ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

On September 13, Trump began publicly calling on Ukraine to stop targeting diesel infrastructure. The following week, Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was also concerned that Ukraine had hit US-linked oil shipments.

Ukraine has refused to halt the strikes, saying its long-range drone campaign is its only viable response to nearly five years of Russian bombardment. Moscow was forced in July to ban diesel exports as part of a raft of measures to address domestic fuel shortages.

Angered by Zelenskiy’s defiance, Trump on October 9 announced a deal to buy diesel from Moscow, issuing a temporary general license that allows Russian diesel to reach the global market. He also waived sanctions on Russia authorized by a bill he signed into law in September.

Suriya Jayanti, a former US official who runs a power sector company in Ukraine, said Russia’s strikes on Ukraine’s power grid have increased, despite Trump unilaterally announcing an energy ceasefire on October 11.

“It is clear to everyone in Kyiv that the goal is not actually an energy ceasefire, but it is really just an effort to hobble Ukraine and give Russia a decisive advantage,” said Jayanti, who is also a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council think tank.

HAS THE US THREATENED TO CUT OFF SUPPORT TO UKRAINE?

Zelenskiy has said Ukrainian military officials had been threatened by US counterparts, who said continuing the energy strikes would lead the US to cut off intelligence sharing. A US official familiar with the situation disputed Kyiv’s account.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, the US official said there has been no increase in pressure on Ukraine.

“We don’t have to pressure Zelenskiy. If he wants to make a deal he’ll make a deal. I think Putin is putting a ton of pressure on him and he (Zelenskiy) is putting some pressure on Russia but Russia doesn’t seem to be minding it as much even though they are getting hit.”

On Thursday, Trump said he had asked SpaceX CEO Elon Musk to restore Ukraine’s access to the company’s Starlink satellite system. Starlink’s disruption temporarily hampered Kyiv’s military drone operations and spurred fears that Kyiv would be left defenseless against Russia’s attacks going into the winter.

WHAT IS THE STATUS OF MOSCOW-KYIV PEACE TALKS?

Peace efforts have continued but so far have not yielded tangible results.

At talks in Oslo on October 20, Ukraine presented new proposals, and Trump’s son-in-law and envoy Jared Kushner repeated Trump’s demand that Ukraine stop attacking Russian diesel refineries.

The next day, envoy Witkoff – a close friend of Trump’s – met Putin in St. Petersburg. Putin agreed to release detained American Stephen Hubbard in what the two countries called a goodwill gesture.

Zelenskiy said on Friday that negotiators from Ukraine, Russia and the US would meet in Abu Dhabi in the first half of November, a possible precursor to a meeting of the three countries’ leaders. The last US-mediated peace talks took place in February.

(Reporting by Steve Holland and Simon Lewis; Editing by Don Durfee and David Gregorio)

The young and the restless—capitalism’s year of discontent

The larger message from the streets may be that the balance between market efficiency and social security has shifted too far.

Pravesh Sharma

25 October, 2026 10:43 am IST

Facebook

Twitter

WhatsApp

Linkedin

A demonstrator kicks a tear-gas-emitting object during a student protest in Brussels, Belgium on Saturday | Reuters

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

S omething unusual is stirring on the streets of the world.

The immediate causes are different. In Bangladesh, a student protest over quotas in public employment grew into something much bigger. In Nepal, restrictions on social media provided the spark, but behind them lay accumulated anger over corruption, economic stagnation, and the conspicuous lifestyles of a privileged political class. Both countries endured extended periods of chaos that resulted in a reset of the political landscape.

India has seen its own manifestations of youth anger, first around entrance examinations and paper leaks, and subsequently about the revision of electoral rolls. Even though the protest e rs in India have remained steadfastly non-violent and do not advocate larger political changes, the government views them with unease. More recently, young people have been prominent in demonstrations, often violent, across France, Belgium, Italy, and Albania.

Show Full Article

There is ostensibly no common organisation linking these movements, no shared manifesto, and certainly no single ideology. Their political circumstances are very different. It would be simplistic to describe them as one global movement. But it would be equally unwise to ignore the common undertow.

Those left behind by the ‘new economy’ Much of the anger stems from a generation beginning to doubt the economic bargain offered to it. For several decades, the legitimacy of market capitalism rested on a relatively simple proposition : Economic growth would create opportunities ; e ducation would enable social mobility ; and h ard work would be rewarded. Each generation could reasonably expect to live somewhat better than the previous one. The state, meanwhile, would provide a reasonable floor of schools, universities, healthcare, transport, and social protection.

That bargain looks increasingly uncertain. Global youth unemployment remains high, with the college-educated cohort disproportionately impacted. But statistics tell only part of the story. Many traditional entry points into secure middle-class employment are shrinking. Young people increasingly encounter temporary work, stagnant incomes, expensive housing, and intense competition for a limited number of secure jobs. They are invited to celebrate the “new economy” and its gig-like character, which many are understandably reluctant to do.

For an educated young person, unemployment is not merely the absence of income. It represents a broken expectation. Families invest heavily in education because they see it as the route to economic mobility. When degrees no longer lead reliably to employment and competitive examinations become lotteries involving millions of applicants, frustration inevitably acquires a political dimension.

This helps explain why education and employment have repeatedly become flashpoints. The youth-led upheaval in Bangladesh began with access to government jobs. The protests in India against paper leaks reflected the enormous stakes attached to a limited number of opportunities. Across parts of Europe, students, teachers, and workers have protested over education funding, wages, and deteriorating public services.

These are d ifferent grievances, certainly, but behind them lurks a single question: what future does society offer its young? This question has become more urgent as economic insecurity coincid es with pressures on the public services on which citizens depend.

Governments everywhere face genuine fiscal constraints. Populations are ageing. Public debt has risen. Healthcare costs are growing. Defence and security expenditure is increasing. In countries such as India, an enormous buildout of economic and social infrastructure is still needed, much of it to be undertaken by the government. These pressures cannot simply be wished away.

Yet, there are political consequences when fiscal adjustment translates into poorer schools, more expensive universities, unaffordable housing, weaker social protection, and increasingly strained healthcare. What appears in a government budget as expenditure rationalisation can seem vastly different to a young citizen struggling to establish an independent life.

Also read: What H&M’s decline and Zara’s growth mean for India’s apparel industry

Time to renew the social contract Parallel to this crisis, another, potentially more unsettling development is taking place: the extraordinary visibility of concentrated wealth. Capitalism has always produced inequality. What has changed is both its scale in some societies and its visibility everywhere. Young people facing insecure employment and uncertain prospects simultaneously inhabit a digital world in which enormous private fortunes and extravagant lifestyles are displayed and lauded continuously. Nepal offers an unusually vivid illustration , where the lifestyles associated with the families of powerful people became a lightning rod for a wider resentment.

But the issue goes beyond conspicuous consumption. Across countries, enormously wealthy individuals and corporations possess growing influence over technology, media, political campaigns, and public debate. Successful enterprise, innovation, and risk-taking remain essential engines of prosperity. Wealth in itself is hardly the problem. The difficulty begins when citizens believe that wealth can purchase disproportionate political influence—or that the rules governing ordinary people do not apply equally to those at the top. Inequality ceases to be a distant economic statistic then, and becomes injustice deeply felt by young people.

A n uncomfortable relationship is emerging between economic discontent and populist politics. In several democracies, sections of the wealthy have found common cause with R ight-wing populist movements promising lower taxes, deregulation, or protection from institutional constraints. Populist leaders have often proved adept at redirecting economic anxiety toward immigration, cultural identity, minorities, or established institutions.

The paradox is striking. Citizens frustrated by economic insecurity can end up supporting political movements whose economic programmes do relatively little to alter the underlying distribution of wealth and opportunity. This is why viewing the current global unrest simply through the familiar prism of ‘ Left versus Right ’ misses something important. Many young protesters do not speak the language of traditional ideology. They speak about jobs, examinations, rent, schools, corruption, dignity, and fairness. They organise through social media rather than political parties or trade unions. Their mobilisation can therefore be sudden, decentralised, and unpredictable.

The fact remains that every street protest can’t be romanticised. Protest movements can appear to be incoherent. Legitimate demonstrations can descend into violence. Social media can amplify misinformation as readily as genuine grievances. Governments have a mandate and responsibility to maintain public order. But maintaining order and understanding discontent are different tasks.

The larger message from the streets may be that the balance between market efficiency and social security has shifted too far. Capitalism has demonstrated an extraordinary ability to generate wealth, innovation, and technological progress. But its political legitimacy ultimately depends on something more: enough people must believe that they have a reasonable opportunity to participate in that prosperity.

The social contract everywhere is in urgent need of renewal. That means restoring opportunity and social mobility; protecting reasonable access to education, healthcare, and housing; ensuring genuine competition rather than entrenched economic power; and maintaining credible boundaries between wealth and political influence. Governments worldwide must recognise that economic growth, while indispensable, cannot be the only measure of a successful society.

Pravesh Sharma is a former IAS officer who served in Madhya Pradesh, the PMO, and the UN. Views are personal.

(Edited by Prasanna Bachchhav)
